An outspoken royalist, Hobbes fled to France during...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Hobbes’s Leviathan as the foundational source for the traditional philosophical definition of David Foster Wallace as one who assumes responsibility and ownership over a text.

book:774783.description: A new collection of interlocking short fictions that pay an irreverent and entertaining fictional tribute to Hollywood myths, from the acclaimed author of The Public Burning and Gerald's Party.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace references Coover’s A Night at the Movies as a post-1985 Image-Fiction text that engages with cinematic and televisual culture.
David Foster Wallace cites Coover’s You Must Remember This as part of the Image-Fiction wave, treating media and memory as intertwined themes.

book:web_31021535.description: A short story by Robert Coover, originally published in 1977 in the collection 'Pricksongs and Descants'. It is a postmodern, experimental narrative that exemplifies Coover's innovative style and use of mythic and folkloric motifs.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace references Coover's novel as an early instance of Imagist tactics, positioning it within the evolution of Image-Fiction.

book:530741.description: Three screenplays by Mike Leigh. Naked presents a bleak picture of urban society, Life is Sweet is a gentle comedy in which the pain of everyday life is borne with a wry smile, and High Hopes is a comedy of class-ridden life in contemporary Britain.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Naked as a film employing Lynchian narrative disjunction through its use of unrelated, unsettling parallel storylines.

book:web_95acbc3c.description: A 1990 book by George Gilder, a prominent technology futurist and conservative thinker, in which he predicts the rise of interactive media and the decline of traditional broadcast television, emphasizing the role of bandwidth and digital networks in transforming American life.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Gilder's book as a representative example of technologically optimistic conservative thought on television, highlighting its commercial packaging and flawed assumptions about consumer agency and technological solutions.
David Foster Wallace cites Maya Deren as an influence on Lynch’s experimental, dreamlike cinematic language.

book:22571704.description: In 1975, Greil Marcus'sMystery Train changed the way readers thought about rock 'n' roll and continues to be sought out today by music fans and anyone interested in pop culture. Looking at recordings by six key artists--Robert Johnson, Harmonica Frank, Randy Newman, the Band, Sly Stone, and Elvis Presley--Marcus offers a complex and unprecedented analysis of the relationship between rock 'n' roll and American culture. In this latest edition, Marcus provides an extensively updated and rewritten Note and Disc...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Marcus's Mystery Train as a significant cultural analysis, likely for its insights into American music and identity.

book:716226.description:
The Language of the Hand
A brand-new edition of the classic work first published in 1894. Cheiro was a renowned palmist whose world travels gained attention in the press and whose palm readings for the rich and famous of his day, including Mark Twain, elicited words of praise. In this unique book are methods for reading personalities, recognizing astrological links, and prognostication, along with drawings of hands showing structural types and lines. A series of photographic hand prints taken directly from....
commentaries: David Foster Wallace references Cheiro’s book as an effective airfoil for biking against the wind, suggesting he found unexpected practical value in a text likely intended for divination or palmistry.

book:16098650.description:
Librarian's Note: this is an alternate cover edition- ISBN 10: 0679745580 (ISBN 13: 9780679745587)
On November 15, 1959, in the small town of Holcomb, Kansas, four members of the Clutter family were savagely murdered by blasts from a shotgun held a few inches from their faces. There was no apparent motive for the crime, and there were almost no clues.
As Truman Capote reconstructs the murder and the investigation that led to the capture, trial, and execution of the killers, he generates both mesmerizing sus...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Truman Capote's In Cold Blood as the source of Robert Blake’s acclaimed 1967 performance, using it to highlight the depth and menace Lynch has revived in Blake’s role.

book:636175.description: The acclaimed author of Free Agents presents a brilliant satire involving a struggle for land in central Florida between three commercial giants; Walt Disney, Howard Johnson, and Margery Post.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace lists Apple’s Propheteers as a post-1985 example of Image-Fiction, highlighting its engagement with public figures and media.

book:490255.description: With this, his famous inaugural collection of stories, Max Apple dives into the mainstream of American culture, and his unfailingly wry depictions of the forces that drive this great nation (greed, lust, perfection, ice cream) make his stories exciting, frightening, and eternally new.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Max Apple’s short story as an early example of projecting interior life onto a pop-culture figure, foundational to Image-Fiction.

book:web_85a89045.description: A play by Bernard Pomerance, first performed in 1977, based on the life of Joseph Merrick, known as the Elephant Man. It was later adapted into a film by David Lynch in 1980.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace references The Elephant Man as a major Lynch film that helped redefine cinematic boundaries during the 1980s blockbuster era.

book:1992048.description: Edited, with an Introduction, by Thomas Bender
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Tocqueville's Democracy in America as a reference point, likely for its analysis of American culture or society.
David Foster Wallace cites Blood Simple as an example of a Coen Brothers film that employs Lynchian chiaroscuro lighting and noir aesthetics.

book:web_cd9d5f9b.description: A seminal work by Fredric Jameson analyzing the relationship between global capitalism, aesthetics, and film, arguing that postmodern cultural forms reflect the logic of late capitalism and geopolitical shifts in the post-Cold War era.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Jameson's books as examples of dense, obscure academic writing, using them to critique the style of contemporary literary scholarship.

book:web_70d50cd3.description: A seminal work of Marxist literary criticism by Fredric Jameson, analyzing structuralism and the limitations of language in literary theory. It critiques Saussurean linguistics and explores the ideological dimensions of narrative form.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Jameson's books as examples of dense, obscure academic writing, using them to critique the style of contemporary literary scholarship.

book:web_2e5f162d.description: A critical work by Fredric Jameson exploring the relationship between visual culture, ideology, and representation in film and media, focusing on how the visible is structured by historical and political forces.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace quotes this specific work to exemplify what he considers obscurantist academic prose, highlighting its syntactic confusion and stylistic excess.

book:310976.description: Since his death in 1989, John Cassavettes has become increasingly renowned as a cinematic hero--a renegade loner who fought the Hollywood system, steering his own creative course in a career spanning thirty years. Having already established himself as an actor, he struck out as a filmmaker in 1959 with Shadows, and proceeded to build a formidable body of work, including such classics as Faces, Woman Under the Influence, The Killing of a Chinese Bookie, and Gloria. In Cassavettes on Cassavettes, Ray Carney p...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Cassavetes as a key influence on Lynch’s raw, emotionally intense filmmaking style.

book:393601.description: Any book-length interview with Alfred Hitchcock is valuable, but considering that this volume's interlocutor is Francois Truffaut, the conversation is remarkable indeed. Here is a rare opportunity to eavesdrop on two cinematic masters from very different backgrounds as they cover each of Hitch's films in succession. Though this book was initially published in 1967 when Hitchcock was still active, Truffaut later prepared a revised edition that covered the final stages of his career. It's difficult to think o...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace acknowledges Hitchcock as one of Lynch’s cinematic influences, though no specific film is cited.

book:484028.description: The hidden story of L.A. Mike Davis shows us where the city's money comes from and who controls it while also exposing the brutal ongoing struggle between L.A.'s haves and have-nots.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites 'City of Quartz' as a concise conceptual key to understanding the film's themes, implying it provides essential context for interpreting Lynch's portrayal of Los Angeles.

book:526770.description:
Enlarged edition, containing 15 stories
"Michael Martone writes with deep affection for the ordinary. In his hands, the quotidian dreams of the American heartland are transformed... " --Louise Erdrich
"This is a marvelous book.... What a gift!" --Richard Rhodes
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Martone’s work as Image-Fiction that interrogates the boundaries of fact and fiction through iconic American figures.

book:web_7d6d4218.description: A critical study of German cinema by British film historian and documentary filmmaker Paul Rotha, originally published as part of his broader work on film history. This essay or chapter appears in his 1976 book 'The German Film: A Critical Study' or similar compilation, though the exact title may vary slightly in different editions.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Paul Rotha's essay as a source for a critical observation about viewers of Expressionist cinema, using it to frame a discussion of David Lynch's visual style.

book:7756245.description: In the jungles of South America, on the ice fields of Alaska, the plains of the Midwest, and the streets of San Francisco, a fearsome battle rages. The insects are vying for world domination; the inventors of electricity stand in evil opposition. Bug , a young man, rebels against his own kind and joins forces with the insects. Wayne, a thug, allies himself with the malevolent forces of electricity and vows to assassinate the preying mantis who tends bar in Oregon. A brusque La Pasionara with the sprightly n...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Vollmann’s novel as a post-1985 Image-Fiction work that uses pop-culture elements in allegorical, almost mythic ways.

book:2065376.description: Here are 13 daring and innovative tales dealing with "skinheads, x-ray patients, whores, lovers, fetishists, and other lost souls" who populate landscapes as diverse as ancient Babylon, India, and contemporary San Francisco. Part fiction, part reportage, these narratives are laced with a bleak and bitter humor, and portray a dazzling array of characters.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Vollmann’s collection as Image-Fiction that anthropomorphizes consumer electronics, embedding them in philosophical frameworks.

book:10864003.description: One morning, as Gregor Samsa was waking up from anxious dreams, he discovered that in bed he had been changed into a monstrous verminous bug." With this startling, bizarre, yet surprisingly funny first sentence, Kafka begins his masterpiece, The Metamorphosis. It is the story of a young traveling salesman who, transformed overnight into a giant, beetle-like insect, becomes an object of disgrace to his family, an outsider in his own home, a quintessentially alienated man. Rather than being surprised at the t...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace uses this story to demonstrate how Kafka literalizes metaphorical expressions of dehumanization, linking everyday language to the narrative’s existential themes.

book:8573943.description: "A Hunger Artist," also translated as "A Fasting Artist" and "A Starvation Artist," is a short story by Franz Kafka published in 1922. The protagonist is an archetype of Kafka, an individual marginalized by society.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace references this story to explore how Kafka transforms psychological and linguistic metaphors into literal narrative conditions, revealing deeper spiritual yearning.

book:26900843.description:
"In the Penal Colony" is a short story by Franz Kafka written in German in October 1914, and first published in October 1919.
The story is set in an unnamed penal colony. It describes the last use of an elaborate torture and execution device that carves the sentence of the condemned prisoner on his skin in a script before letting him die, all in the course of twelve hours. As the plot unfolds, the reader learns more and more about the machine, including its origin, and original justification.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Kafka’s story as an example of authority figures that are absurd, scary, and sad, using it to illustrate the layered tone of Kafka’s humor.

book:1106138.description: Welcome to Mark Leyner'sAmerica, where you can order gallium arsenide sushi at a roadside diner, get loaded on a cocktail of growth hormones and anabolic steroids, and support your habit by appearing on TV game shows. Here is fiction the brain can dance to, by one of the funniest and most subversive young writers of this, or any other, decade.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Leyner’s novel as an extreme example of Image-Fiction, using hyper-saturated pop-culture fragments to mimic media overload.
David Foster Wallace cites Mark Leyner's novel as a cultural phenomenon among campus hipsters, positioning it as a literary response to televisual culture that celebrates rather than resists it.

book:web_f526067e.description: A collection of short stories by American writer Stephen Dixon, published in 1993 by Henry Holt and Company. The book features fragmented, emotionally intense narratives often exploring themes of loss, memory, and domestic life.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace references Dixon’s collection as an Image-Fiction work that explores the intersection of film and narrative form.

book:32991063.description: Robert Bresson, the director of such cinematic master-pieces as Pickpocket, A Man EscapedMouchette, and L'Argent, was one of the most influential directors in the history of French film, as well as one of the most stubbornly individual: He insisted on the use of nonprofessional actors; he shunned the "advances" of Cinerama and Cinema-Scope (and the work of most of his predecessors and peers); and he minced no words about the damaging influence of capitalism and the studio system on the still-developing--in....
commentaries: David Foster Wallace identifies Bresson as a stylistic influence on Lynch, particularly in his use of restrained, almost mechanical acting.

book:440003.description: Krazy Kat adores Ignatz Mouse. She sees the bricks he hurls at her head as tokens of love, and each day Ignatz arranges a cunningly different method of delivery for his missile. But when Ignatz and Krazy witness the mega-brick explosion in the desert, Krazy becomes depressed, and refuses to perform. To coax her back to work so they can regain their lost limelight, Ignatz invents his own brand of psychotherapy, orchestrates her kidnapping, and tries to seduce Krazy with promises of stardom from a Hollywood p...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Cantor’s Krazy Kat as a post-1985 Image-Fiction work that reimagines pop-culture icons in literary form.

book:web_1cec2369.description: A scholarly work by H. L. Hix, originally published as a Ph.D. dissertation and later released as a book by Temple University Press in 1992 as part of their 'The Arts and Their Philosophies' series. It explores the death of the author in postmodern literary theory, engaging with thinkers like Barthes and Foucault.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Hix’s book as a significant 1990s critical work that engages with poststructuralist theory, particularly Barthes’ 'Death of the Author.'

book:web_14e710a9.description: A 1996 action-horror film written by Quentin Tarantino and directed by Robert Rodriguez. It is not a book but a movie, often referenced in pop culture discussions. The citation mistakenly treats it as a book, but it is a cinematic work.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites From Dusk to Dawn as a commercially driven film that lacks Lynch’s depth, used to underscore Lynch’s artistic superiority.

book:5988858.description: Three years on the New York Times bestseller list, CODEPENDENT NO MORE first identified attitueds, feelings, and behaviors now recognized as hallmarks of codependency. Checklists, activities, and self-tests provide concrete tasks to help readers examine the nuances of codependency in their lives.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace notes an older passenger reading this book, implicitly associating it with the emotional dynamics of cruise passengers, though without elaborating on its content or author's ideas.

book:web_292fb8bd.description: A 1994 American comedy film written, directed, and produced by the Coen Brothers. It stars Tim Robbins, Jennifer Jason Leigh, and Paul Newman. The film is a satirical homage to 1940s screwball comedies and corporate culture.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace includes The Hudsucker Proxy as another Coen Brothers film exhibiting Lynchian visual and tonal influences, particularly in lighting and mood.

book:18816.description:
During his time in Leningrad, Bakhtin shifted his focus away from the philosophy characteristic of his early works and towards the notion of dialogue. It is at this time that he began his engagement with the work of Dostoevsky. Problems of Dostoyevsky's Artis considered to be Bakhtin's seminal work, and it is here that Bakhtin introduces three important concepts.
First, is the concept of the unfinalizable self: individual people cannot be finalized, completely understood, known, or labeled. Though it is pos...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace states that Frank critiques Bakhtin’s interpretation of Dostoevsky by appealing to historical evidence rather than theoretical frameworks.
David Foster Wallace cites Bakhtin’s work as a politically constrained interpretation of Dostoevsky’s polyphonic style, which downplayed his ideological commitments under Soviet censorship.

book:6324725.description: "Politics and the English Language" (1946) is an essay by George Orwell that criticises the "ugly and inaccurate" written English of his time and examines the connection between political orthodoxies and the debasement of language. The essay focuses on political language, which, according to Orwell, "is designed to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable, and to give an appearance of solidity to pure wind." Orwell believed that the language used was necessarily vague or meaningless because it was in...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Orwell’s essay as the definitive critique of academic jargon, affirming its enduring relevance despite its age.
David Foster Wallace references Dostoevsky’s The Idiot as an example of problematic translation choices in Constance Garnett’s English version.
David Foster Wallace indicates that Frank treats The Idiot as a central text in his analysis of Dostoevsky’s moral and spiritual themes during his most productive period.

David Foster Wallace cites Dostoevsky's The Idiot as an example of a serious, morally passionate novel in which a character delivers a deeply philosophical monologue — contrasting it with contemporary fiction's aversion to such earnestness.
David Foster Wallace references The Idiot to illustrate Dostoevsky’s narrative technique and apparent avoidance of detailing key plot developments, highlighting a stylistic quirk.

book:5695.description:
Inspired by the true story of a political murder that horrified Russians in 1869, Fyodor Dostoevsky conceived of Demons as a "novel-pamphlet" in which he would say everything about the plague of materialist ideology that he saw infecting his native land. What emerged was a prophetic and ferociously funny masterpiece of ideology and murder in pre-revolutionary Russia.
~penguinrandomhouse.com
commentaries: David Foster Wallace emphasizes that Frank treats Demons as a major ideological text, central to understanding Dostoevsky’s critique of radicalism in 1860s Russia.

book:web_d2f0a699.description: A novel by Fyodor Dostoevsky, originally published in 1872 as 'Besy' in Russian, exploring political radicalism, nihilism, and religious faith in 19th-century Russia. It is also known in English as 'Demons'.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace notes that Frank uses the title 'The Devils' to refer to Dostoevsky's novel, highlighting the variability in English translations of Dostoevsky's works.

book:web_4b5ead4a.description: A philosophical novella by Fyodor Dostoevsky, considered a precursor to existentialism, exploring themes of alienation, free will, and the irrationality of human behavior through the monologue of an isolated narrator.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Notes (presumably Notes from Underground) as a key text illustrating Dostoevsky’s critique of egoistic atheism and its psychological consequences.

book:139421.description: The Eternal Husband (Russian: Vechnyi muzh, Vechny muzh) is a novel by Russian author Fyodor Dostoyevsky that was first published in 1870 in Zarya magazine. The plot revolves around the complicated relationship between Velchaninov and Trusotsky, the husband of his deceased former lover.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace notes that Frank includes The Eternal Husband among the key works analyzed to demonstrate Dostoevsky’s engagement with psychological and moral dilemmas.

book:15829603.description:
Alternate Cover of ISBN 9780140444568
In January 1850 Dostoyevsky was sent to a remote Siberian prison camp for his part in a political conspiracy. The four years he spent there, startlingly re-created in "The House of the Dead", were the most agonizing of his life. In this fictionalized account, he describes his soul-destroying incarceration through the cool, detached tones of his narrator, Aleksandr Petrovich Goryanchikov: the daily battle for survival, the wooden plank beds, the cabbage soup swimming wit...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites House of the Dead as the foundational text through which Dostoevsky developed his critique of liberal paternalism toward the Russian peasantry.

book:6316119.description: Set in Russia in the midst of its troubled transition to the modern age, this classic novel is the profound human drama of Raskolnikov, a sensitive intellectual driven by poverty and the belief of his exemption from moral law. Through his unforgettable gallery of characters, Dostoyevsky provides a provocative look at the human motivations of obsession and possession with unflinching philosophical and moral insight. A masterpiece of dramatic literature by one of the greatest novelist of all time.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace notes that Joseph Frank dedicates substantial analysis to Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment as part of his effort to foreground the novels themselves in his biographical study.
David Foster Wallace contrasts Crime and Punishment with Tolstoy’s The Death of Ivan Ilych to highlight Dostoevsky’s nuanced, non-reductive treatment of moral and spiritual transformation.
David Foster Wallace cites Crime and Punishment as an example of awkward English phrasing in modern translations, questioning the fidelity and readability of the rendered text.

book:11057575.description:
The final masterpiece from the celebrated author of "Crime and Punishment" and "The Idiot."..
This extraordinary novel, Dostoyevsky s last and greatest work, tells the dramatic story of four brothers Dmitri, pleasure-seeking, impatient, unruly . . . Ivan, brilliant and morose . . . Alyosha, gentle, loving, honest . . . and the illegitimate Smerdyakov, sly, silent, cruel. Driven by intense passion, they become involved in the brutal murder of their own father, one of the most loathsome characters in all lite...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace lists The Brothers Karamazov among Dostoevsky’s major novels, noting their thematic focus on murder and tragedy without deeper interpretive commentary.

David Foster Wallace cites The Brothers Karamazov as a central work in which Dostoevsky develops his theological vision through the character of Zossima, tied to his encounter with Holbein’s painting.

book:6568440.description: Dostoevsky's most revolutionary novel, Notes from Underground marks the dividing line between nineteenth- and twentieth-century fiction, and between the visions of self each century embodied. One of the most remarkable characters in literature, the unnamed narrator is a former official who has defiantly withdrawn into an underground existence. In full retreat from society, he scrawls a passionate, obsessive, self-contradictory narrative that serves as a devastating attack on social utopianism and an asserti...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace references Dostoevsky's Notes from Underground as a key text whose parodic function and ideological context are central to Frank's biographical analysis.
David Foster Wallace uses a direct quote from the Pevear and Volokhonsky translation of Notes from Underground to critique the unnatural English syntax and stylistic choices in modern translations.

David Foster Wallace cites Dostoevsky’s Notes from Underground as the starting point for Joseph Frank’s scholarly engagement with Dostoevsky’s work, highlighting its psychological complexity and historical context.

book:640363.description: When Poor Folkwas first published in 1846, Dostoyevsky -- one of nineteenth-century Russia's most important authors -- was just twenty-four years old. The novel brought him immediate critical and public acclaim. A poignant societal and physiological sketch, Dostoyevsky's masterpiece is written in the form of letters of correspondence between two characters, both trapped within the poverty and circumstance of St. Petersburg's slums. Makar is a writer struggling to survive; Varvara, a low-paid seamstress. The...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Poor Folk as an early example of Dostoevsky’s engagement with social realism and its reception by the socialist Left.

book:11180973.description: Psychologically probing novel concerns the gambling episodes, tangled love affairs and complicated lives of Alexey Ivanovitch, a young gambler; Polina Alexandrovna, the woman he loves; a pair of French adventurers and other characters. Bleak picture of the fatal attractions of gambling with wonderful characterization, faithful depiction of gambling life at fashionable German watering holes.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace highlights that Frank includes close readings of Dostoevsky’s The Gambler, treating it as integral to understanding David Foster Wallace’s ideological development.
David Foster Wallace references The Gambler to show how Dostoevsky explores the corrosive influence of European secularism on Russian identity and moral character.

book:2263960.description: THE POORHOUSE FAIR was John Updike's first full length novel, published four years after he graduated from Harvard. It concerns the events surrounding a fair put on by members of a poorhouse and is an allegory about charity. Short and succinct, it speaks to those fears all of us have of growing not old, but dependent. "Since the successful poetic novel--for lack of a more precise term--has long been the most rarefied form of prose fiction, John Updike, the poet and short story writer, has done a startling t...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites this early novel as one of Updike’s masterpieces, contrasting it with his later works to show a decline in quality.
David Foster Wallace identifies this novel as a turning point where Updike’s characters became more repellent, marking the beginning of a perceived moral and emotional decline in his fiction.

book:666916.description: In John Updike's fourth and final novel about ex-basketball player Harry "Rabbit" Angstrom, the hero has acquired heart trouble, a Florida condo, and a second grandchild. His son, Nelson, is behaving erratically; his daughter-in-law, Pru, is sending out mixed signals; and his wife, Janice, decides in midlife to become a working girl. As, through the winter, spring, and summer of 1989, Reagan's debt-ridden, AIDS-plagued America yields to that of George Bush, Rabbit explores the bleak terrain of late middle a...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites this novel as a moment when Updike began to more openly confront his own mortality, signaling a shift toward darker, more personal themes.

book:85384.description:
WINNER OF THE NATIONAL BOOK AWARD AND THE PRIX DU MEILLEUR LIVRE ETRANGER
The Centaur is a modern retelling of the legend of Chiron, the noblest and wisest of the centaurs, who, painfully wounded yet unable to die, gave up his immortality on behalf of Prometheus. In the retelling, Olympus becomes small-town Olinger High School; Chiron is George Caldwell, a science teacher there; and Prometheus is Caldwell's fifteen-year-old son, Peter. Brilliantly conflating the author's remembered past with tales from Gree...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace elevates this novel to the status of a classic, positioning it as a high point in Updike’s career before his later decline.

book:2258155.description: In this short novel, Joey Robinson, a thirty-five-year-old advertising consultant employed in Manhattan, describes the visit made by himself, his newly acquired second wife, and his eleven-year-old stepson to the farm where he grew up and where his mother now lives alone. For three days, a quartet of voices explores the air, relating stories, making confessions, seeking alignments, quarreling and pardoning. They are not entirely alone; ghosts--fathers, lovers, children--press upon them, and an increasingly....
commentaries: David Foster Wallace includes this novel among Updike’s acclaimed early works, suggesting it exemplifies his literary strength before his later self-absorption.

book:760653.description: Ben Turnbull, the hero of John Updike's eighteenth novel, is a sixty-six-year-old retired investment counselor living north of Boston in the year 2020. A recent war between the United States and China has thinned the population and brought social chaos. The dollar has been locally replaced by Massachusetts scrip; instead of taxes, one pays protection money to competing racketeers. Nevertheless, Ben's life, traced by his journal entries over the course of a year, retains many of its accustomed comforts, as s...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace references this novel as a late work by Updike that explores apocalyptic themes and personal mortality, while criticizing it as clunky and self-indulgent.
David Foster Wallace uses this novel as a primary example of Updike’s late-career solipsism, highlighting its autobiographical protagonist and thematic preoccupation with death.
David Foster Wallace cites this book as the low point in Updike’s oeuvre, using it to justify a broader critique of his later work’s self-indulgence.

book:400690.description:
John McCain is one of the most admired leaders in the United States government, but his deeply felt memoir of family and war is not a political one and ends before his election to Congress. With candor and ennobling power, McCain tells a story that, in the words of Newsweek, "makes the other presidential candidates look like pygmies."
John McCain learned about life and honor from his grandfather and father, both four-star admirals in the U.S. Navy. This is a memoir about their lives, their heroism, and the....
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites this book as a source of inspiration for a young boy, indicating its role in shaping political ideals and personal admiration for McCain.

David Foster Wallace cites McCain’s memoir as a strategic component of his 2000 campaign, suggesting it was used to reinforce an image of authenticity while being part of a calculated marketing effort.

book:web_256f79f7.description: A comprehensive reference guide to modern legal terminology, usage, and style, widely regarded as an authoritative resource for lawyers, judges, and legal writers.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Garner's earlier dictionary as a foundational work that established his reputation in usage scholarship.

book:344645.description: This book - a detailed explanation and defense of standard American English - contains more than 700 pages of crisp, authoritative guidance on hundreds of questions of grammar and usage. "A Dictionary of Modern American Usage" treats all these topics and more: basic grammar, as well as advanced nuances; word preferences and shades of meaning; punctuation; idiomatic phrases; spelling; and effective style. In an age of linguistic uncertainty, this book gives surefooted guidance on the direct, precise, and rob...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace references Garner’s preface to support the claim that SNOOT tendencies are hereditary, citing Garner’s personal and genetic observations.
David Foster Wallace cites Garner’s dictionary as a significant and comprehensive modern usage guide, highlighting its rhetorical and ideological strengths.

David Foster Wallace praises Garner's dictionary as a superior and balanced work in the field of usage guides, highlighting its thoroughness and its author's rhetorical restraint as key to its authority.

David Foster Wallace argues that Garner's genius lies not in the comprehensiveness of his dictionary but in his rhetorical strategy of neutral, disinterested presentation, which sidesteps the pitfalls of prescriptive elitism.

David Foster Wallace credits Garner with reviving a viable form of linguistic authority by embodying a lowercase, disinterested objectivity that transcends postmodern skepticism, making his dictionary a rhetorical triumph.

David Foster Wallace cites Garner's dictionary as a model of technocratic authority, praising its ethical appeal and its successful redefinition of linguistic authority through reason, experience, and rhetorical persuasion rather than dogmatism.
David Foster Wallace cites Bryan Garner's dictionary as a sophisticated and modern resource that navigates usage debates with strategic insight.
David Foster Wallace critiques Garner's treatment of vogue words in this usage manual, noting that Garner's analysis is superficial and occasionally incorrect.

book:915353.description:
Which is preferred - nom de plume, pseudonym, or pen name? What are neologisms, disguised conjunctions, and fused participles? Language enters into almost every part of human life and yet it is all too often misused: directness and clarity disappear in a whirl of cliches, euphemisms, and wooliness of expression.
Janet Whitcut has revised Eric Partridge's popular reference book to reflect the language of well-informed writers, readers, and speakers today. She has also added a section to the book entitled "Vo...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace describes Garner’s formative encounter with Partridge’s book as a pivotal moment that ignited his lifelong passion for English usage.
